A.title: Cap the refugee charge and tie it to ability to pay
A.answer: Keep the Bill's contribution mechanism, which the government says applies to asylum seekers in taxpayer-funded accommodation who can afford to pay (s2), but replace the flat £10,000 charge on refugees (s1) with an income-tested contribution under a fixed cap. The Home Office would assess means at the point of grant and collect only from earnings. Free food, money and a bed would stay in place while a claim is decided. Amendments at report stage (s1) would set this in the Bill. It worked if repayments are collected without causing destitution, and if the Home Office publishes yearly collected sums against collection costs. Simulated citizens backed an ability-to-pay cap (27 backers) and a no-destitution limit (36).

B.title: Take refugee repayment out of the Home Office's hands
B.answer: Drop the flat £10,000 charge on refugees who received asylum support (s1). The government says the Bill lets it require asylum seekers in taxpayer-funded accommodation to contribute when they can afford to (s2). Give that affordability test to an independent assessor, not the department that runs the asylum system. Parliament fixes a cap; the assessor sets income-based amounts, publishes every decision, and collects only through tax once someone works. Success: no one left without money, food or a bed while waiting, which 36 simulated citizens backed as a limit, and published figures show how much is recovered against what collecting it costs.
